disclaimer: This is general guidance only and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist. Local regulations and approved practices may vary.
description: Phytophthora in guava is caused by water mould-like organisms that thrive in poorly drained, waterlogged soil. It primarily attacks the root system and the base of the trunk (collar region), causing dark, water-soaked lesions that girdle the tree and cut off its ability to absorb water and nutrients. Affected trees show wilting, yellowing of leaves, sudden dieback of branches, and general decline — even when the soil appears moist. The disease can also cause a brown rot on fruit. It spreads rapidly through infected soil, irrigation water, and surface runoff.
immediate_actions: Improve drainage around the affected tree immediately — remove standing water and avoid over-irrigation.
Do not waterlog the root zone of affected or neighbouring trees.
Examine the base of the trunk for dark, discoloured, or sunken bark — scrape carefully with a clean tool to check.
Avoid moving soil, water, or plant material from the infected area to other parts of the grove.
Consult a local agricultural extension officer urgently for guidance on approved management options — severely affected trees may not recover.
spread_prevention: Ensure the orchard has good drainage infrastructure — Phytophthora cannot establish without waterlogged conditions.
Avoid planting guava in low-lying areas prone to flooding or poor drainage.
Do not reuse soil or water from areas where Phytophthora has been confirmed.
Clean and disinfect footwear, tools, and equipment before moving between the infected area and healthy parts of the grove.
Use raised planting mounds or beds in areas with heavy clay soil to keep the root crown well above the waterline.
Use certified, disease-free planting material from reputable nurseries.
long_term_monitoring: Inspect the trunk base and root zone of all trees regularly, especially after heavy rainfall.
Monitor tree canopy health — sudden wilting or unexplained yellowing in well-watered trees is an early warning sign.
Keep records of affected trees and observe whether the problem is concentrated in low-lying or poorly drained parts of the grove.
Discuss long-term drainage improvement and replanting strategies with a local agricultural extension officer.
Avoid replanting susceptible guava varieties in areas where Phytophthora has been confirmed without expert guidance.
